L1179: Implementation note
L1180: This spec, as with many CSS specs, has been written to prioritize understandability over efficiency. A number of algorithms, notably the above "parse as a declaration, then parse as a rule" behavior can be fairly inefficient if implemented naively as described.
L1181: 
L1182: However, the behavior has been carefully written to allow "early exits" as much as possible. In particular, and roughly in order of when the exit can occur:
L1183:   * If the first non-whitespace token isn’t an cite154†<ident-token> for a recognized property name (or a custom property name), you can immediately stop parsing as a declaration and reparse as a rule instead. If the next non-whitespace token isn’t a cite202†<colon-token> , you can similarly immediately stop parsing as a declaration.
L1184: 
L1185: (That is, font+ ... is guaranteed to not be a property, nor is not-a-prop-name: ....)
L1186:   * If the first two non-whitespace tokens are a custom property name and a colon, it’s definitely a custom property and won’t ever produce a valid rule, so even if the custom property ends up invalid there’s no need to try and reparse as a rule.
L1187: 
L1188: (That is, --foo:hover {...} is guaranteed to be a custom property, not a rule.)
L1189:   * If the first three non-whitespace tokens are a valid property name, a colon, and anything other than a cite131†<{-token> , and then while parsing the declaration’s value you encounter a <{-token>, you can immediately stop parsing as a declaration and reparse as a rule instead.
L1190: 
L1191: (That is, font:bar {... is guaranteed to be an invalid property.)
L1192:   * If you see a recognized property name, a colon, and a {}-block, but the first non-whitespace tokens following that block isn’t either immediately the final semicolon, or the !important followed by the semicolon, you can immediately stop parsing as a declaration and reparse as a rule instead.
L1193: 
L1194: (That is, cite325†font: {} bar ... is guaranteed to be an invalid property; you don’t need to keep parsing until you hit a semicolon.)
L1195: Similarly, even tho the parsing requirements are specified to rely on checking the grammar of the declarations as you parse, a generic processor trying to implement a non-CSS language on top of the generic CSS syntax can still get away with just verifying that declarations start with an ident, a colon, and then either contain solely a {}-block or no {}-block at all. They’ll just spent a little more time on parsing than an implementation with grammar knowledge in cases like foo:hover ...
L1196: {}, since they can’t early-exit on the first token.

L1341: ## 6. The `An+B` microsyntax
L1342: 
L1343: Several things in CSS, such as the cite339†:nth-child() pseudoclass, need to indicate indexes in a list. The `An+B` microsyntax is useful for this, allowing an author to easily indicate single elements or all elements at regularly-spaced intervals in a list.
L1344: 
L1345: The An+B notation defines an integer step (`A`) and offset (`B`), and represents the `An+B`th elements in a list, for every positive integer or zero value of `n`, with the first element in the list having index 1 (not 0).
L1346: For values of `A` and `B` greater than 0, this effectively divides the list into groups of `A` elements (the last group taking the remainder), and selecting the `B`th element of each group.
L1347: 
L1348: The `An+B` notation also accepts the even and odd keywords, which have the same meaning as 2n and 2n+1, respectively.
L1349: 
L1350: Examples:
L1351: 
L1352:     2n+0   /* represents all of the even elements in the list */
L1353:     even   /* same */
L1354:     4n+1   /* represents the 1st, 5th, 9th, 13th, etc. elements in the list */
L1355: The values of `A` and `B` can be negative, but only the positive results of `An+B`, for `n` ≥ 0, are used.
L1356: 
L1357: Example:
L1358: 
L1359:     -1n+6   /* represents the first 6 elements of the list */
L1360:     -4n+10  /* represents the 2nd, 6th, and 10th elements of the list */
L1361: 
L1362: 
L1363: If both `A` and `B` are 0, the pseudo-class represents no element in the list.
L1364: ### 6.1. Informal Syntax Description
L1365: 
L1366: This section is non-normative.
L1367: 
L1368: When `A` is 0, the `An` part may be omitted (unless the `B` part is already omitted). When `An` is not included and `B` is non-negative, the cite340†+ sign before `B` (when allowed) may also be omitted. In this case the syntax simplifies to just `B`.
L1369: 
L1370: Examples:
L1371: 
L1372:     0n+5   /* represents the 5th element in the list */
L1373:     5      /* same */
L1374: 
L1375: When `A` is 1 or -1, the `1` may be omitted from the rule.
L1376: 
L1377: Examples:
L1378: The following notations are therefore equivalent:
L1379: 
L1380:     1n+0   /* represents all elements in the list */
L1381:     n+0    /* same */
L1382:     n      /* same */
L1383: 
L1384: If `B` is 0, then every `A`th element is picked. In such a case, the `+B` (or `-B`) part may be omitted unless the `A` part is already omitted.
L1385: 
L1386: Examples:
L1387: 
L1388:     2n+0   /* represents every even element in the list */
L1389:     2n     /* same */
L1390: 
L1391: When B is negative, its minus sign replaces the cite340†+ sign.
L1392: 
L1393: Valid example:
L1394: 
L1395:     3n-6
L1396: Invalid example:
L1397: 
L1398:     3n + -6
L1399: 
L1400: Whitespace is permitted on either side of the cite340†+ or - that separates the `An` and `B` parts when both are present.
L1401: 
L1402: Valid Examples with white space:
L1403: 
L1404:     3n + 1
L1405:     +3n - 2
L1406:     -n+ 6
L1407:     +6
L1408: 
L1409: Invalid Examples with white space:
L1410: 
L1411:     3 n
L1412:     + 2n
L1413:     + 2
L1414: ### 6.2. The `<a-n-plus-b>` type
L1415: 
L1416: The `An+B` notation was originally defined using a slightly different tokenizer than the rest of CSS, resulting in a somewhat odd definition when expressed in terms of CSS tokens. This section describes how to recognize the `An+B` notation in terms of CSS tokens (thus defining the `<a-n-plus-b>` type for CSS grammar purposes), and how to interpret the CSS tokens to obtain values for `A` and `B`.

L734:       1. cite11†Optionally report an error .
L735:     2. Else,
L736:       1. Let `offset` be cite19†JSONObjectGet (`section`, "offset").
L737:       2. If `offset` is not a cite110†JSON object , throw an error.
L738:       3. Let `offsetLine` be cite19†JSONObjectGet (`offset`, "line").
L739:       4. Let `offsetColumn` be cite19†JSONObjectGet (`offset`, "column").
L740:       5. If `offsetLine` is not an cite122†integral Number , then
L741:         1. cite11†Optionally report an error .
L742:         2. Set `offsetLine` to +0_{𝔽}.
L743:       6. If `offsetColumn` is not an cite122†integral Number , then
L744:         1. cite11†Optionally report an error .
L745:         2. Set `offsetColumn` to +0_{𝔽}.
L746:       7. Let `offsetPosition` be a new cite23†Position Record { `[[Line]]`: `offsetLine`, `[[Column]]`: `offsetColumn` }.
L747:       8. If `previousOffsetPosition` ≠ null, then
L748:         1. If cite25†ComparePositions (`offsetPosition`, `previousOffsetPosition`) is lesser, cite11†optionally report an error .
L749:       9. If `previousLastMapping` ≠ null, then
L750:         1. If cite25†ComparePositions (`offsetPosition`, `previousLastMapping`.`[[GeneratedPosition]]`) is lesser, cite11†optionally report an error .
L751:         2. cite188†NOTE : This part of the decoding algorithm checks that entries of the cite187†sections field of index source maps are ordered and do not overlap. While it is expected that generators should not produce index source maps with overlapping sections, source map consumers may, for example, only check the simpler condition that the section offsets are ordered.
L752:       10. Let `mapField` be cite19†JSONObjectGet (`section`, "map").
L753:       11. If `mapField` is not a cite110†JSON object , throw an error.
L754:       12. Let `decodedSectionCompletion` be cite90†Completion (cite29†DecodeSourceMap (`json`, `baseURL`)).
L755:       13. If `decodedSectionCompletion` is a cite87†throw completion , then
L756:         1. cite11†Optionally report an error .
L757:       14. Else,
L758:         1. Let `decodedSection` be `decodedSectionCompletion`.`[[Value]]`.
L759:         2. For each cite129†Decoded Source Record `additionalSource` of `decodedSection`.`[[Sources]]`, do
L760:           1. If `sourceMap`.`[[Sources]]` does not contain `additionalSource`, then
L761:             1. Append `additionalSource` to `sourceMap`.`[[Sources]]`.
L762:         3. Let `offsetMappings` be a new empty cite121†List .
L763:         4. For each cite134†Decoded Mapping Record `mapping` of `decodedSection`.`[[Mappings]]`, do
L764:           1. If `mapping`.`[[GeneratedPosition]]`.`[[Line]]` = 0, then
L765:             1. Set `mapping`.`[[GeneratedPosition]]`.`[[Column]]` to `mapping`.`[[GeneratedPosition]]`.`[[Column]]` + `offsetColumn`.
L766:           2. Set `mapping`.`[[GeneratedPosition]]`.`[[Line]]` to `mapping`.`[[GeneratedPosition]]`.`[[Line]]` + `offsetLine`.

L768:         5. Set `sourceMap`.`[[Mappings]]` to the cite189†list-concatenation of `sourceMap`.`[[Mappings]]` and `offsetMappings`.
L769:         6. Set `previousOffsetPosition` to `offsetPosition`.
L770:         7. If `offsetMappings` is not empty, set `previousLastMapping` to the last element of `offsetMappings`.
L771:     3. Return `sourceMap`.

L773: Implementations may choose to represent index source map sections without appending the mappings together, for example, by storing each section separately and conducting a binary search.
L774: # 11 Retrieving source maps
L775: # 11.1 Linking generated code to source maps
L776: 
L777: While the source map format is intended to be language and platform agnostic, it is useful to define how to reference to them for the expected use-case of web server-hosted JavaScript.
L778: 
L779: There are two possible ways to link source maps to the output. The first requires server support in order to add an HTTP header and the second requires an annotation in the source.
L780: Source maps are linked through URLs as defined in cite5†WHATWG URL ; in particular, characters outside the set permitted to appear in URIs shall be percent-encoded and it may be a data URI. Using a data URI along with sourcesContent allows for a completely self-contained source map.
L781: 
L782: The HTTP `sourcemap` header has precedence over a source annotation, and if both are present, the header cite97†URL should be used to resolve the source map file.
L783: Regardless of the method used to retrieve the cite190†source map URL the same process is used to resolve it, which is as follows.
L784: 
L785: When the cite190†source map URL is not absolute, then it is relative to the cite98†generated code 's source origin. The cite191†source origin is determined by one of the following cases:
L786:   * If the generated source is not associated with a script element that has a `src` attribute and there exists a `//# sourceURL` comment in the cite98†generated code , that comment should be used to determine the cite191†source origin .
L787: 
L788: Note
L789: 
L790: Previously, this was `//@ sourceURL`, as with `//@ sourceMappingURL`, it is reasonable to accept both but `//#` is preferred.
L791:   * If the cite98†generated code is associated with a script element and the script element has a `src` attribute, the `src` attribute of the script element will be the cite191†source origin .
L792:   * If the cite98†generated code is associated with a script element and the script element does not have a `src` attribute, then the cite191†source origin will be the page's origin.
L793:   * If the cite98†generated code is being evaluated as a string with the `eval()` function or via `new Function()`, then the cite191†source origin will be the page's origin.
L794: # 11.1.1 Linking through HTTP headers
L795: 
L796: If a file is served through HTTP(S) with a `sourcemap` header, the value of the header is the cite97†URL of the linked source map.
L797: 
L798:     `sourcemap: <url>`
L799: 
L800: Note
L801: 
L802: Previous revisions of this document recommended a header name of `x-sourcemap`. This is now deprecated; `sourcemap` is now expected.
L803: # 11.1.2 Linking through inline annotations
L804: 
L805: The cite98†generated code should include a comment, or the equivalent construct depending on its language or format, named `sourceMappingURL` and that contains the cite97†URL of the source map. This specification defines how the comment should look like for JavaScript, CSS, and WebAssembly. Other languages should follow a similar convention.
L806: For a given language there can be multiple ways of detecting the `sourceMappingURL` comment, to allow for different implementations to choose what is less complex for them. The cite98†generated code unambiguously links to a source map if the result of all the extraction methods is the same.
L807: 
L808: If a tool consumes one or more source files that cite192†unambiguously links to a source map and it produces an output file that links to a source map, it shall do so cite192†unambiguously .
L809: 
L810: Note
L811: The following JavaScript code links to a source map, but it does not do so cite192†unambiguously :
L812: 
L813:     `let a = `
L814:     //# sourceMappingURL=foo.js.map
L815:     // ``
L816: 
L817: Extracting a cite190†source map URL from it cite193†through parsing gives `foo.js.map`, while cite194†without parsing gives null.
L818: # 11.1.2.1 JavaScriptExtractSourceMapURL ( `source` )
L819: 
L820: The abstract operation JavaScriptExtractSourceMapURL takes argument `source` (a String) and returns a String or null. It extracts a cite190†source map URL from a JavaScript source. It has two possible implementations: either cite193†through parsing or cite194†without parsing .
L821: 
L822: To extract a cite190†source map URL through parsing:
